source: Dalal, Santos, Valentino, Freitas, Cunningham (2024) Inferring the Best Explanation? IBE-Eval: LLM-generated explanations scored with inference-to-the-best-explanation criteria
finding: Code can compute four IBE virtues on LLM-written explanations: logical consistency (solver), parsimony (proof depth, concept drift), coherence, and linguistic uncertainty (hedging). Combined, they pick the better explanation in causal multiple choice well above chance and beat a GPT-3.5 judge.
numbers: Best composed accuracy 77% (about 27 points over 50% random, +17 over GPT-3.5-as-judge) on COPA and E-CARE with GPT-3.5, Llama 2 13B and Llama 2 7B as explainers. Average gain over judge +17.5 points across models and tasks.
quote: IBE-Eval, which considers all IBE criteria, improves the ability to select the best explanation by 17%
limits: Only two-option causal commonsense tasks; needs two competing explanations; scores are not calibrated across unrelated items.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S7: rank candidate explanations by code-computed virtues, not by a model judge (supports G5).

source: Dalal, Santos, Valentino, Freitas, Cunningham (2024) Inferring the Best Explanation? IBE-Eval: LLM-generated explanations scored with inference-to-the-best-explanation criteria (single-virtue results)
finding: Logical consistency is almost useless as a signal: models write consistent explanations for wrong answers as often as for right ones. They over-rationalize by adding premises.
numbers: Consistency alone near chance (Table 1 values about .50 to .55 for most model/task pairs; some .61 to .63). Parsimony beat consistency by an average of 14 points. Proof depth and concept drift were 6% and 10% higher on average for the incorrect option; the gap grew with model size.
limits: Small models (7B to GPT-3.5). Gap by size is a trend over three models only.
agent_relevance: A fluent, consistent story is cheap for an LLM to produce for any hypothesis. Consistency of an explanation must never count as a pass; supports G3 and G10. Extra assumptions are a usable code-side warning sign.

source: Dalal, Santos, Valentino, Freitas, Cunningham (2024) Inferring the Best Explanation? IBE-Eval: LLM-generated explanations scored with inference-to-the-best-explanation criteria (hedging and human check)
finding: Models hedge more when explaining the weaker option. Linguistic uncertainty was the strongest single predictor. IBE-Eval scores agree with human choice far better than a GPT-3.5 judge does.
numbers: Uncertainty added +13 points on COPA and +4 on E-CARE. Humans (2 raters, 100 pairs) picked the correct-answer explanation 96% (COPA) and 91% (E-CARE), kappa .68. Spearman with human choice: IBE-Eval 0.64 (p<.01), GPT-3.5 judge 0.31 (not significant).
limits: Hedging may be a style artifact of these models; not tested on newer reasoning models. Human sample is 100 pairs.
agent_relevance: Counting hedge words and added concepts in a candidate explanation is a free signal for S7 ranking, but test on our own model first [S].

source: Sun and Saparov (2025, v3 2026) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? An Evaluation of Parsimony in Inductive and Abductive Reasoning
finding: Synthetic ontology worlds with hidden facts: the model must propose hypotheses that explain all observations. With one hypothesis and shallow trees, models do well. With several hypotheses and deeper trees, accuracy collapses, and valid-but-not-simplest hypotheses are common.
numbers: 100 generated items per setting. Multi-hypothesis accuracy fell from above 80% at tree height 1 to below 50% at height 2 for all models except GPT-4o, though true hypotheses rose only from 3.0 to 3.5. At height 4 all models kept at least 20% weak accuracy but very low strong accuracy and quality.
limits: Synthetic fictional worlds, not real science. Paper says success here does not imply real-world success.
agent_relevance: Weak accuracy (explains the data) is the easy bar; the Occam-quality bar is hard. A code check of 'explains all observations' is not enough; add a minimality score in code (G5).

source: Sun and Saparov (2025, v3 2026) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? An Evaluation of Parsimony in Inductive and Abductive Reasoning (prompt and model effects)
finding: Reasoning models and buffer-of-thought prompting beat plain chain-of-thought, but a persistent gap stays between weak accuracy (explains) and strong accuracy (explains and is simplest). In-distribution demonstrations help; out-of-distribution demonstrations do not.
numbers: GPT-5.4 and o3 beat Llama3-70B at every height. BoT usually above CoT, mostly in weak accuracy. 8-shot in-distribution demos raised strong accuracy and quality at heights 3 and 4. SFT of Qwen3-4B on the synthetic data: strong accuracy +11.0 points at height 1, +8.5, +4.0, +1.5 at height 4.
limits: Gains shrink with depth. SFT is out of scope for our no-training agent.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples must match the problem's shape; generic prompt tricks do not close the parsimony gap.

source: Sun and Saparov (2025, v3 2026) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? An Evaluation of Parsimony in Inductive and Abductive Reasoning (error types)
finding: Four recurring failure types in abduction: wrong direction of the rule (all mammals are cats), ignoring the ontology and adding needless hypotheses, falling back to the observation itself as the hypothesis, and inventing entities copied from demonstrations.
numbers: Described in Section 4.5 and Appendix I; the trivial-hypothesis fallback is flagged as low quality because it only explains itself.
limits: Qualitative categories from manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Cheap code checks for S4: reject a hypothesis equal to an observation, reject entities absent from the problem, test rule direction on a held-out case (G3).

source: Qiu et al. (2024, ICLR) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement
finding: A propose-test-refine loop is the closest published LLM version of Peirce's cycle. GPT-4 proposes natural-language rules, a symbolic interpreter filters them against the examples, and failures feed the next round. It beats direct input-output prompting, self-consistency, and self-refine.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy: IO 64.0, SC(N=5) 65.0, self-refine(T=3,N=5) 70.0, refinement T=3,N=5 82.5. ACRE task accuracy: IO 28, SC 29, SR 32, refinement 59. MiniSCAN task accuracy: IO 0.0, refinement T=3,N=1 46.0. GPT-4-0613, temperature 0.7 for multiple hypotheses.
quote: both iterative refinement and external feedback are essential
limits: Gains depend on a task-specific symbolic interpreter. MiniARC raw accuracy was lower with refinement (18.7) than IO (33.1).
agent_relevance: Same shape as S3 to S5: generate several hypotheses, test with a program, revise from the real failing output. Direct support for G2 and G4.

source: Qiu et al. (2024, ICLR) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement (no-feedback ablations)
finding: Voting over more samples did not help, and using the LLM itself as the interpreter in place of code erased most of the gain. More hypotheses per round helped because selection by an external check filters them.
numbers: Self-consistency barely moved over IO (ACRE 64.0 to 65.0). Self-refine with LM interpreter reached only 70.0 raw / 32 task on ACRE versus 82.5 / 59 with the symbolic interpreter. T=3,N=1 beat T=3,N=5 on MiniSCAN, which the authors blame on overfitting to the shown examples.
limits: One model (GPT-4), four datasets.
agent_relevance: Confirms G1, G2, G5 and G3: the check must be code, and fit to the shown examples can mislead (overfit selection).

source: Qiu et al. (2024, ICLR) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement (rule induction vs rule application)
finding: The model proposes rules it cannot reliably apply. When the LM applies its own rules instead of the interpreter, accuracy drops, sometimes to near zero. Humans find LM rules comparably clear on easy tasks but worse on hard ones.
numbers: MiniSCAN task accuracy fell from above 80% with the symbolic interpreter to almost zero with the LM interpreter. Human pairwise comparison of rule clarity and supportiveness: LM rules clearly worse on MiniARC; inter-annotator kappa 0.13 for clarity, 0.53 for supportiveness. Noisy exemplars hurt the LM more than humans.
limits: Pairwise human study with small samples; kappa for clarity is low.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis written in words is not evidence that the model can use it. Test hypotheses by executing them as code where possible (G3, G10).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) UNcommonsense Reasoning: Abductive Reasoning about Uncommon Situations
finding: Abduction for unlikely outcomes. Human-written explanations are the least preferred, LLM-written (GPT-4, 3-shot) are better, and human explanations polished by an LLM are best. The mix trades human specificity against LLM diversity.
numbers: 20,947 context-outcome pairs. Pairwise human preference vs GPT-4 explanations, un-SocialIQA: Crowd win 30.8%, C+LLM 43.2%, LLM2 33.8%; un-RocStories: 19.2, 28.4, 26.4. Fleiss kappa 0.43 to 0.55. C+LLM preference grew as the outcome got less likely. GPT-3 few-shot preferred over GPT-4 only 13% of the time.
limits: Preference judged by crowd workers, not by truth. Giving the LLM the human instructions helped on one dataset and hurt on the other.
agent_relevance: Models can already write plausible explanations for strange facts; the weak step is picking among them, not producing them. Supports separate generate and select states.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) UNcommonsense Reasoning: Abductive Reasoning about Uncommon Situations (imitation learning)
finding: Small open models trained by plain supervised fine-tuning on GPT-4 explanations lose to GPT-4. Online imitation (expert-as-oracle, SED) cuts the lose rate. Not reproducible by prompting alone.
numbers: Absolute 10% win-rate gain vs the GPT-4 baseline for the best imitation methods; LLaMA-7B SFT non-lose rate 48% and FlanT5-XXL 44% vs GPT-4.
limits: Training-based; outside our no-training scope.
agent_relevance: Low direct value; shows the ceiling for small models is training, not scaffold.

source: He et al. (2025) GEAR: A General Evaluation Framework for Abductive Reasoning
finding: Single-gold-answer scoring hides that abduction is underdetermined. GEAR scores a set of hypotheses by code, with no labels: consistency with the observations, generalizability (does it predict unseen inputs), and diversity of predictions.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 4 benchmarks (Mini-ARC, ACRE, List Functions, ARC), 1,500 problems, 50,340 hypotheses. Only about 20% of hypotheses from 70B-class models were consistent. Around 80% of equally plausible hypotheses were labelled incorrect by gold-answer scoring. Model size only weakly related to diversity.
quote: existing gold-answer evaluations overlook the underdetermination inherent to abduction
limits: Needs a checkable hypothesis form (executable rules). Gold-label comparisons were not run against human judges.
agent_relevance: Matches our design: judge hypotheses by running them on held-out cases (G3, G8). Also warns against forcing one answer too early: keep a diverse pool until a test splits them.

source: He et al. (2025) GEAR: A General Evaluation Framework for Abductive Reasoning (does a higher score predict truth?)
finding: In a simulation, the hypothesis with the higher GEAR score (more generalizable and diverse) was more likely to pass hidden observations, odds ratio above 1 in most settings, drifting toward 1 as more hidden cases were used.
numbers: Odds ratio of passing hidden cases, chosen vs rejected, above 1 in most cells for m=1..4 hidden cases and context sizes 0 to 2. Preference-trained 7B models (Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, NextCoder-7B): top-3 accuracy rose, e.g. Llama-3.1-8B top-1 0.000 to 0.035, Qwen 0.035 to 0.066.
limits: Explicit odds ratios are only plotted in Figure 4 and not tabulated in text. Training numbers small.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a computed virtue (prediction coverage) tracks truth on held-out cases, which answers the 'do virtues track truth' question in a measurable way for code tasks.

source: Liu, Neubig, Andreas (2024) An Incomplete Loop: Deductive, Inductive, and Abductive Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Tested the Peirce cycle in four LMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, Llama-2-7b and 70b) on linear functions, color words, and Kalamang translation. Instruction inference (abduction) beats few-shot only in simple cases and hurts in hard ones. Ability to induce a good rule is mostly unrelated to ability to learn from examples.
numbers: Given the true instruction, GPT-4-turbo went from 30% to 96% on linear functions. Spearman between true and induced coefficients, GPT-4-turbo b: 0.85, a: 0.91; GPT-3.5 b: 0.27, a: 0.56; Llama models near zero. Kalamang vocabulary induction only 10-20% for most models; grammar features 4-5 of 18 correct.
quote: the ability to learn through abduction (proposing hypotheses) is generally not related to learning through induction
limits: Small models by 2026 standards. Authors note many Llama hypotheses were incoherent.
agent_relevance: Writing a hypothesis does not predict that the model can use or learn it. Do not assume a generate-then-apply loop works; measure each link (G7). A correct stated rule helps a lot (deduction is strong), so the verified-rule step in S8 is worth the cost.

source: Salimi et al. (2026) Wiring the 'Why': A Unified Taxonomy and Survey of Abductive Reasoning in LLMs
finding: First survey with a compact benchmark. Splits abduction into Stage I generation and Stage II selection. Selection is nearly mature on short tasks; long narrative and open-ended generation stay hard; models stay below humans.
numbers: Stage II: ART 87.2 and e-CARE 88.0 (GPT-5.4; humans 91.4 and 92.0); DDXPlus top-1 79.75, hit@3 98.7; True Detective best 42.9 (human average 47%); MuSR murder best 68.0 (GPT-4o; human 92.1). Qwen2.5 3B to 72B on ART: 65.8, 75.8, 83.6.
limits: Authors used restricted subsets, one direct prompt, models of their choice; numbers not comparable to published results on the same sets.
agent_relevance: Choosing among given candidates is easy; generating the right candidate is the bottleneck. Spend scaffold budget on S3 generation breadth and on code-side tests.

source: Salimi et al. (2026) Wiring the 'Why': A Unified Taxonomy and Survey of Abductive Reasoning in LLMs (generation stage)
finding: Open-ended generation of explanations is far weaker than selection. Strongest model gets only about 21.5% on ProofWriter abductive statements, and about 63 hit@3 on diagnosis.
numbers: GPT-5.4: ProofWriter accuracy 21.5, F1 61.6; AbductionRules 99.6; NeuLR 70.8; UNcommonsense win rate vs enhanced crowd references 61.5; DDXPlus hit@3 63.0, Set-F1@3 28.1. Llama3.1 8B: ProofWriter 1.5. GPT-4o still led GPT-5.4 on MuSR and some generation metrics.
limits: Single-run numbers; LLM judge used for some tasks (DDXPlus matching, UNcommonsense).
agent_relevance: Large spread across tasks means we need a task-class gate (S0) before spending on abduction operators.

source: Salimi et al. (2026) Wiring the 'Why': A Unified Taxonomy and Survey of Abductive Reasoning in LLMs (abduction vs deduction and induction)
finding: Pooling published experiments, abduction sits between deduction and induction, and strong deduction does not predict strong abduction.
numbers: Median accuracy: deduction 79.96%, abduction 42.50%, induction 28.8%. Most abduction-vs-deduction pairs were below 50% abductive but above 60% deductive.
limits: Pooled from three papers (Sheng 2025, Dougrez-Lewis 2025, Xu 2025) with mixed methods and datasets; authors call it cautious.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a reasoning-strong model is good at hypothesis generation; test the abduction step separately.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models
finding: Syllogisms turned into abduction (choose the premise that explains the conclusion, or 'neither'). Models do poorly, are biased to always pick an explanation, and show belief bias like humans. Few-shot help is very uneven.
numbers: n=216. Zero-shot overall: GPT-3.5 31.0, GPT-4 41.7, Llama3-8B 37.5, Llama3-70B 37.0; 'Neither' answers near 0-12%. Few-shot: GPT-4 28.7 (worse), Llama-3-70B 75.5 with 63% on Neither. Deduction zero-shot GPT-4 72.2, few-shot 95.8. GPT-4 chose a Negative sentence 67.9% of the time though only 16.7% were correct. Inconsistent-with-belief items about 10 points lower.
limits: Old models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4-0613, Llama 3); abstract format; few-shot behavior not stable.
agent_relevance: Models rarely say 'none of these explains it'. This is the 'bad lot' failure; our threshold must be enforced in code with a no-good-enough exit, not asked of the model (G6, G8).

source: Shi et al. (2023) Language Models Can Improve Event Prediction by Few-Shot Abductive Reasoning (LAMP)
finding: A working abduction-in-a-loop system: an event model proposes a future event, the LLM suggests causes from a few expert demonstrations, a search module finds matching past events, and a learned scorer checks whether they could cause the proposal. The final ranking is adjusted by the score.
numbers: On GDELT predicate-object joint prediction the true type moved from rank about 40 to about 20. On ICEWS object prediction mean rank improved from about 90 to about 20. 95% bootstrap CIs very tight. GPT-3.5 and Llama versions much better than GPT-3.
limits: Improvement shown on ranking among a base model's proposals; needs a trained scorer and retrieval over event history. Gains grew with more proposals but retrieval count has an optimum (5 to 10).
agent_relevance: Concrete pattern for S3 to S4: model explains from the effect back to causes, code retrieves evidence for each cause, a separate scorer decides (G5, G8).

source: Luo et al. (2026, ICML) Graph of States: Solving Abductive Tasks with Large Language Models
finding: Deduction-style frameworks (CoT, ToT, GoT, FoT) fail on open abductive tasks (diagnosis, fault finding) in four ways: evidence fabrication, context drift, failed backtracking, early stopping. GoS keeps an explicit causal graph of hypotheses and evidence and a state machine that controls drill-down, backtracking and termination.
numbers: Medical diagnosis, human judge: GoS Match 39.86%, Relevant 78.99% vs best baselines about 26% Match (Multi/FoT at $0.73 per case vs GoS $0.12). Distributed-system failure diagnosis: GoS Match 70.67%, Relevant 88.00%, +36.67 and +1.33 over best baseline. Ablation Match: full 31.88 (LLM judge), without reasoning focus 19.57, without causal graph 18.12, without state machine 12.32.
limits: Two real-world datasets; baselines adapted by the authors; LLM judge favors surface similarity (human scores higher). Table layout in the PDF text is partly misaligned, so baseline numbers are approximate.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that code-held state (hypothesis list with support and refute marks, thresholded transitions) beats free-form tree search for abduction (G1, G2, G7). Maps onto our S4 to S6.

source: Luo et al. (2026, ICML) Graph of States: Solving Abductive Tasks with Large Language Models (termination thresholds)
finding: A confidence-gap threshold before drilling deeper trades precision for conservatism: moderate thresholds improve correctness, very high thresholds make the agent stop at a shallow diagnosis. Without a state machine the agent burns the whole budget.
numbers: Cost without state machine rose to $0.17 per case from $0.12. GoS beat the best baseline's peak performance even with a restricted iteration and retrieval budget.
limits: Threshold values tuned per dataset.
agent_relevance: Use a code-checked margin between top two hypotheses as the stop rule, not a model's feeling of confidence (G1, G12).

source: Abdaljalil et al. (2025) Theorem-of-Thought: A Multi-Agent Framework for Abductive, Deductive, and Inductive Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Three role-prompted agents (abductive, deductive, inductive) each write a reasoning graph; an NLI model scores coherence and the best graph wins. Small gains on small models; self-consistency did surprisingly badly in their runs.
numbers: Single decoding pass, seeds fixed, 7B models. WebOfLies 5-statement: ToTh 43% vs CoT-greedy 19%, self-consistency 38%, CoT-decoding 46%. ToTh +29 points over CoT-greedy on Mistral-7B for WebOfLies. Self-consistency only 14% (DeepSeek-7B) on WebOfLies. Not a clean abduction test.
limits: Not abduction in the IBE sense: WebOfLies and MultiArith are deduction and arithmetic. No ablation of the abductive agent alone. Persona-style agents conflict with our G4/G9.
agent_relevance: Weak. Shows role-split agents are not shown to help on abduction; avoid persona voters (G4, G9).

source: Lin (2025) Abductive Inference in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models: Generating and Validating Missing Premises
finding: Pipeline: detect that retrieved evidence is insufficient, generate candidate missing premises, validate them with an NLI model and retrieval checks. Reports gains over plain RAG.
numbers: HotpotQA F1: LLM-only 51.2, RAG 67.8, FiD 71.4, HyDE 72.0, abductive RAG 75.3. EntailmentBank EM 61.5 vs RAG 54.3 (+7.2). ART human plausibility 4.1 vs 3.1.
limits: Single independent-researcher preprint; the paper's index terms mention static analysis, a sign of template reuse; no seeds, CIs or compute-matched baseline. Treat as weak [S].
agent_relevance: Idea is useful: a 'missing premise' operator triggered only when a check shows the evidence is insufficient (G1). Numbers unreliable.

source: Wang, McCoy, Steinert-Threlkeld (2024) Minimization of Boolean Complexity in In-Context Concept Learning
finding: Open LLMs learn simpler Boolean concepts better than complex ones, like humans (Feldman's finding). This is a learning bias toward simplicity, not an explicit use of parsimony as a selection rule.
numbers: 18 concepts per complexity class. Accuracy fell with complexity: Gemma-2-9B 83% to 66%, Qwen2-72B 90% to 74% (class 1 to 5). Pearson r with complexity: Gemma-2-9B -0.961 (p=.009), Gemma-2-27B -0.898, Qwen2-7B -0.884, Qwen2-72B -0.854 (p=.065).
limits: Only 5 complexity classes, so correlations rest on 5 points. Concept learning, not explanation choice.
agent_relevance: A simplicity prior is partly built in, so a code-side minimality score adds a second, independent signal rather than duplicating the model's own bias.

source: Imran, Lamb, Atkinson (2025) Out-of-Context Abduction: LLMs Make Inferences About Procedural Data Leveraging Declarative Facts in Earlier Training Data
finding: Fine-tuned models on descriptions of fictitious chatbots, then asked which chatbot produced observed replies. GPT-4o could pick the right persona in one of three cases; GPT-4o mini failed. Weak evidence of abduction from training facts.
numbers: GPT-4o: Pangolin persona chosen 84% after seeing German replies vs a prior of 49%; next most frequent persona about 1%. No support for the other two personas or for GPT-4o mini.
limits: 1 of 3 personas, 1 of 2 models; authors note possible catastrophic forgetting and token-length confounds.
agent_relevance: Low relevance to the agent loop. Shows that posterior shifts toward the explaining hypothesis exist but are fragile.

source: Pareschi (2023) Abductive Reasoning with the GPT-4 Language Model: Case studies from criminal investigation, medical practice, scientific research
finding: Interview-style anecdotes with GPT-4 on medical, criminal and cosmology puzzles; the author judges the hypotheses plausible.
numbers: No numbers, no baseline, no blinded judging.
limits: Case studies only; self-judged by the author. Not evidence of reliability.
agent_relevance: Do not use as support. Listed so the weak literature is flagged.

source: Farmer (2026) Abduction Without a Body? Representational Grounding and the Abduction Loop for Scientific Hypothesis Generation
finding: Proposes a six-stage loop (representation, motif extraction, canonical form, cross-domain retrieval, identity hypothesis, adversarial verification) with abstention as the default when verification is inconclusive. One motivating case; no measured results; benchmark DAB-30 deferred to a companion paper.
numbers: No performance numbers. Abstract page read only.
limits: Architecture proposal, single-author preprint; evidence is one anecdote.
agent_relevance: Interesting default (abstain unless verified) but conflicts with our G6 (never abstain on first pass); keep the adversarial-check stage only.
